01 / The challenge

The challenge for food & drink.

When a van is serving, customers should still see the name and understand what’s on offer from the queue. Use the wrap for your permanent identity and keep frequently changing menus and prices on a separate surface.

01

The open hatch

Serving hatches and awnings hide part of the design while you trade.

02

Changing menus

Prices and specials change. Printing them on the wrap means reprinting later.

03

Food photos at scale

Low-resolution food photos look poor when printed large.

02 / What to include

What your van must say.

  • Business name
  • What you serve, in a few words
  • Social handles
  • Website or booking details for events

Not sure what to include? Our guide to what to put on a work van walks you through it.

See how the graphics could work.

Illustrative vehicle graphics concepts.

04 / Recommended package

A printed full wrap for a trading vehicle.

Use a full wrap when photography or illustration needs to carry across the body. A partial wrap works when your base colour already suits the brand.

06 / Design tips

Build the layout around the job.

01

Design for the open hatch

Check the proof with the hatch shown in its serving position.

02

Leave menus easy to update

Reserve a separate board or changeable panel for prices and seasonal offers.

03

Check image quality at scale

Supply original product photography and make sure it still reads at queue distance.

Before you book

Good to know.

Can you wrap a catering trailer?

Send photos, dimensions and details of vents, hatches and trim so we can confirm suitable panels.

How do we keep the menu flexible?

We can plan the wrap around a separate menu board or agree a panel for graphics you expect to replace.

Is vinyl food-safe near the hatch?

The wrap goes on the outside of the vehicle only. Your interior and serving surfaces are not affected.
